claims.text: The initial material can be an as-deposited, nanocrystalline, equimolar CuMoTaWV high-entropy-alloy film.
The as-deposited film has high hardness.
The as-deposited film suffers from poor adhesion.
The as-deposited film has relatively high friction and wear under sliding.
Post-deposition annealing at approximately 300°C can be used to improve adhesion of a CuMoTaWV film.
Annealing in a mildly oxidizing atmosphere promotes copper segregation to the alloy surface.
The proposed annealing treatment produces a thin, continuous Cu-rich oxide layer.
The Cu-rich surface oxide is Cu2O or CuO.
The treatment improves adhesion between the oxide and the underlying nanocrystalline alloy matrix.
During annealing, copper diffuses to the surface and partially oxidizes.
The resulting copper-rich oxide has low shear strength and acts as a solid lubricant.
The copper-rich oxide lowers the coefficient of friction during sliding.
The copper-rich oxide acts as a barrier against wear.
Improved oxide adhesion minimizes spallation under mechanical loading.
A thin, continuous Cu-rich oxide layer can remain stable from room temperature to at least approximately 300°C.
The treatment will reduce room-temperature coefficient of friction by an estimated 30–50% relative to the untreated alloy.
The treated material will maintain lower friction and wear rates than the untreated material up to approximately 300°C.
The untreated alloy has a room-temperature coefficient of friction of approximately 0.5 or higher.
The intervention requires sufficient copper content in the alloy.
Excessive annealing temperature causes adverse oxide thickening, whereas insufficient temperature produces inadequate copper segregation or oxidation.

contradictions.description: The boundary calls the proposed process an 'interstitial modification,' but the intervention and mechanism describe copper segregation and surface oxidation rather than incorporation of interstitial species.
